clue.text: Kiss almost half confusedly in rather public meeting place? (10, two words)

indicators.note: a little under half of a thirteen-letter phrase is kept, so most of it is thrown away

parts.note: buss is an old word for a kiss
helter-skelter means in a confused, disorderly way

explanation.surface: A couple's half-hearted, fumbling kiss in a place where everyone can see them.
explanation.walkthrough: HELTER is six of the thirteen letters of HELTER-SKELTER, so 'almost half'. The question mark admits that a bus shelter is only loosely a meeting place, and a rather public one.
explanation.definitionFit: People wait together under a roadside bus shelter, so it serves, jokingly, as a meeting spot open to every passer-by.

clue.text: Computer standard: after university biblical Jewish leader dis-penses with old mouse!

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A computer standard drops the old mouse, as a scholar of scripture might.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'dis-penses' hints at a pun on pens, but the phrase just means does without.
explanation.definitionFit: Unicode is the international standard that gives every written character a number for computers.

clue.text: Insignificant drudge

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as one description of a lowly worker, but each is a separate sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrub is used adjectivally for anything stunted or paltry, and as a noun for a lowly, overworked person.

clue.text: Small herring — James maybe catches one of a pair in Galilee

explanation.walkthrough: 'James' suggests the fisherman apostle, but it is Sid James, the gravel-voiced star of the Carry On comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Sild are young herring, typically canned as sardines in Norway.

clue.text: Snag again bedevilling arch etc

parts.note: taken as written

clue.text: A Romeo, energy-charged, given a healing juice (8, two words)

clue.text: Not much of a tail but making some runs, cutting

explanation.surface: A cricket side whose tail is weak but still scores a few runs with cut shots.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the tail is the weak late-order batting and a cut is a scoring stroke, so the whole clue reads as cricket; the answer is just an animal's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short upright tail of a hare, rabbit or deer, barely a tail at all.

clue.text: Beetle, oddly secluded without earth

parts.note: taken as written

clue.text: Spar blended with a bit of emerald or quartz

clue.text: Future alternative for tragic hero

second meaning: one of the two choices Hamlet weighs in his famous soliloquy

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet asks whether 'to be, or not to be'; the first of his two options supplies the second sense.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, the to-be means what is still to come, and it is also Hamlet's first option, existing rather than dying.

clue.text: Foster-parents joined a conspiracy

parts.note: met means joined up with
taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: The word is Hebrew: metapelet, plural metaplot, the carers who raise children in a kibbutz.
explanation.definitionFit: On a kibbutz, metaplot were the nurses who brought up the children in place of their parents.

clue.text: Encourage old woodman by turning most of timber measure

indicators.note: turning round makes the little word face the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The small word 'of' does double work: it is read backwards and also connects 'most' to the timber measure.
explanation.definitionFit: To foster is to promote or nurture; foster is also an obsolete contracted form of forester.

clue.text: Like some crosses from Easter formerly in fashion? The opposite

parts.note: Pace is an old and dialect name for Easter, as in pace-egg

explanation.surface: Crosses seen at Easter that were once fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, Easter goes in fashion; 'The opposite' says fashion goes in Easter instead.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry, a cross patonce has arms that widen into three-pointed ends, so it describes a kind of cross.

clue.text: US rascal goes downhill fast, we hear, awfully sick

explanation.surface: An American scamp hurtles down a slope and ends up feeling terribly ill.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeesicks, also spelt skeezicks, is American slang for a rogue or mischievous fellow, a rascal.

clue.text: Beginning of month in Rome — day in, ankle's throbbing

indicators.note: a throbbing ankle is in a disturbed state, so its letters are thrown about

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for day
taken as written, with the s

explanation.surface: At the start of a month in Rome, after a day of sightseeing, someone's ankle aches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'day in' simply puts the letter in with the rest before they are scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: The kalends was the first day of each month in the ancient Roman calendar.

clue.text: Strange taste in bundle where fuel's stored

clue.text: Shakespearean scoffs stale stuff for scoff in seats

to scoff is to eat greedily
corn is trite, old-fashioned material

explanation.walkthrough: The word 'scoff' appears twice: first meaning to jeer, then to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorns, as nouns for taunts or acts of mockery, are used in this sense by Shakespeare.

clue.text: Indian clerk around start of Raj

parts.note: opening letter of the word

clue.text: Starts to purchase at the centre of Macau? This'll help

clue.text: Infants topped Christmas tree?

clue.text: From the off there's very little of value in a cheer? The opposite (5, two words)

clue.text: One can be stripped and free, in euphoria, to mate
